To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we present a distributed, virtual force based, algorithm for self-deployment and event relocation, that is effective in both the deployment phase and in the event relocation phase.
a virtual force-based distributed algorithm can achieve the optimal performance of a centralized solution, with the added advantage of being able to adapt to changing conditions.

we propose an algorithm that allows a mobile wireless network to relocate itself in response to the occurrence of a phenomenon, and that the proposed algorithm is distributed, and achieves a performance comparable to the optimal solution.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of distributed control algorithms to achieve self-deployment, relocation and reconfiguration in mobile wireless sensor networks.
the design of a distributed, scalable, and efficient algorithm for self-deployment and reconfiguration in mobile wireless sensor and actuator networks.
the development of distributed control algorithms for wireless networks that are both self-organizing and self-deploying.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proposed approach is a very effective, simple and distributed algorithm for self-deployment and self-reconfiguration of a wireless network of sensors and actuators.
the proposed approach is a promising one for the design of distributed sensor relocation algorithms, and it can be used as a starting point for the design of more sophisticated algorithms.
this paper proposes a distributed algorithm for the self-deployment and the relocation of nodes in wireless sensor networks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a distributed sensor relocation scheme for environmental control.
we have proposed a unified, distributed scheme for self-deployment and event-driven relocation in wireless sensor-actuator networks.

we propose a unified, decentralized algorithm for the deployment and relocation of a wireless sensor/actuator network that achieves the following objectives: (1) a uniform node deployment; (2) a proper relocation of nodes to sample and control the physical phenomenon; and (3) a uniform node distribution when the phenomenon ends.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, by exploiting the sensing and actuation capabilities of the nodes, it is possible to achieve a very good performance in terms of event detection and control, while maintaining a regular network structure.
a single algorithm is sufficient to achieve the dual objectives of self-deployment of the nodes, and of relocation upon the occurrence of an environmental event.
a distributed algorithm can be designed to achieve a good performance in a variety of scenarios, without the need for any centralized coordination.
